vignette:
Alex sits with a stillness that seems carefully constructed, his hands resting on his knees as if to keep them from moving. He speaks in the precise, logical manner of a man who spends his days managing complex systems. For fifteen years, he has been a database administrator, a digital architect who builds order out of chaos. He found a deep satisfaction in it, in the clean lines of code and the certainty that for every problem, there was a query, a patch, a solution. His world was one of predictable inputs and outputs.

That world shattered two years ago on a Tuesday afternoon. He was in a meeting, explaining a data migration plan, when a sharp, searing pain shot through his chest. He remembers trying to take a breath and finding no air, a terrifying sensation he describes as “drowning on dry land.” The next hours were a blur of panicked colleagues, the jarring wail of a siren, and the blindingly bright lights of the emergency room. The diagnosis was a massive bilateral pulmonary embolism. He had, the doctors later told him, been minutes from death.

He spent nine days in the ICU, a lifetime tethered to a symphony of machines that beeped and whirred, each sound a reminder of his body’s profound betrayal. He felt a complete loss of control, a passive object being acted upon by doctors, nurses, and technology he didn’t understand. His body, once a reliable vehicle for his mind, had become a hostile and alien landscape.

When he was discharged, everyone told him how lucky he was. His wife at the time, Sarah, threw a small “welcome home” party. He smiled, accepted the hugs, and felt nothing but a hollow echo where relief should have been. He tried to return to normal, to his job, to his life. But the architecture of his mind had been corrupted.

At work, the hum of the server room, once a comforting sound of productivity, now mimics the low drone of the ICU monitors. He finds himself staring at a screen of code, but his mind is replaying the image of a doctor’s grim face or the feeling of the ventilator tube being removed from his throat. A sudden tightness in his chest, likely from anxiety, sends a jolt of pure terror through him. He has to lock himself in a bathroom stall, breathing deliberately, convincing himself he is not dying all over again. He has started making small, uncharacteristic errors at work—a missed semicolon, a slow query—and the fear of causing a system crash, of losing control, is constant.

He avoids anything that might trigger the memories. He takes a twenty-minute detour to work to avoid driving past the hospital. He changes the channel if a medical drama comes on. More profoundly, he avoids his own body. He lives on the surface of his skin, terrified of what’s happening inside. A simple cough, a leg cramp, a moment of breathlessness after climbing the stairs—each is a potential harbinger of another clot. He’s constantly, subtly, checking his pulse, monitoring his breathing.

The man who once built and maintained stable relationships now feels entirely disconnected. Sarah left him last year. “It’s like you survived,” she told him, her voice breaking, “but you never really came home. I’m living with a ghost.” He knew she was right. The capacity for joy, for connection, for simple presence, felt like a deleted file he couldn’t recover. He now lives alone in a sparse apartment that feels more like a waiting room than a home. He is alive, his body functions, but he is trapped in the aftermath, endlessly running a diagnostic on himself, waiting for the system to fail again.
